newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine Jan tax collection bodes well for 1997.
newsitem.headline: Argentine Jan tax collection bodes well for 1997.

text.p: Argentine tax collection in January bodes well for government revenues this year and will help the country meet its deficit target agreed with the International Monetary Fund.
"This is a very good figure for Argentine markets in general," said Sergio Galvan, head of research at local bank Bansud.

The Economy Ministry announced late Monday that January tax revenues totaled $4.36 billion, 12.7 percent higher than in the same month a year earlier. They were 13.9 percent higher than in December, when revenues totaled $3.83 billion. By
Including contributions for pension funds, total fiscal revenue was $4.74 billion, 13.9 percent higher than January 1996.
Apart from surpassing analysts' expectations, the figure was the highest ever for the month of January. The average forecast by analysts in a Reuters poll was $4.01 billion.
The increases were particulary noteworthy given that inflation is very low in Argentina. The consumer price index rose only 0.2 percent in calendar year 1996,

"The (tax collection) figures were higher than expectations. We now have to see if the higher level of collections continues, something which is very probable," said Agustin Etchebarne, chief analyst at C&E Consultores.

Although the figure was above expectations, analysts pointed out that collection in January is traditionally boosted by higher than usual income tax payments. Argentine workers are paid their monthly salary 13 times a year and half of that payment is made in January and the other half in July.

Analysts say there are a number of special factors that pushed revenues higher in January. For instance, value-added tax collected by the customs service rose considerably from January last year, largely thanks to reductions in tax reimbursements introduced recently.
Value-added tax collected by customs rose 36.2 percent from January 1996 to $591 million. An increase in the fuel tax also boosted collections by a huge 160.9 percent to $361 million.

Another point, said analysts, is that Argentines who take their summer holidays in January are spending more of their time off in Argentina rather than travelling to Brazil which has become more expensive because of the high value of its real currency.
But, despite these special factors, analysts agree the deepening recovery is paying off for the government's coffers.

"Either way, the figure was higher than expected, and it may continue thanks to increased economic activity and if greater efforts are made to control tax evasion," said Ines Piccinino, an economist at Asesores Economicos.
"This figure confirms the strong economic growth cycle Argentina's economy is in. It also justifies the gains in financial markets recently," said Galvan.
Jose Rutman, an economist at Broda consultants, pointed out that the figure was also in line with the government's forecast of a $4.5 billion budget deficit for the year.
